Monarch Tractor has appointed Steve Peck as Chief Revenue Officer (CRO) to expand sales and accelerate growth in the ag robotics sector.
Key Takeaways:
 Monarch Tractor raised approximately $220–242 million in total funding, including a $133 million Series C in July 2024 — described at the time as the largest-ever raise in agricultural robotics.
 The company developed the MK-V, marketed as the world’s first fully electric, driver-optional, autonomous smart tractor for agriculture.
 By early 2026, Monarch had laid off nearly all remaining staff, vacated its Livermore, California headquarters, and auctioned off equipment.
 The company faces multiple lawsuits over autonomy claims and reportedly attempted a pivot toward a licensing and software business model before the latest round of staff reductions.
 Key partners included Foxconn, Dairy Farmers of America, Verizon Business, and Scout, among others.
Monarch Tractor: A Well-Funded Agricultural Tech Startup Faces an Uncertain Future
Monarch Tractor, the Livermore, California-based startup behind the MK-V electric autonomous tractor, is facing serious questions about its future after a series of developments that have left the company with little visible sign of active operations. Its headquarters has been vacated and listed for lease, equipment has been auctioned, and reports indicate nearly all remaining staff have been laid off — this for a company that was valued at more than $500 million less than two years ago. What comes next, if anything, remains unclear.
The MK-V and the Case for Electric Autonomous Tractors
What Monarch Built
Monarch’s flagship product, the MK-V, was positioned as the world’s first fully electric, driver-optional, autonomous smart tractor designed for agricultural use. The tractor targeted specialty crop operations including vineyards, orchards, berry farms, and dairy, as well as broader land management applications. Early production took place at the company’s Livermore facility before manufacturing shifted to Ohio under a partnership with Foxconn.
Commercial Reach
At its peak, Monarch had established commercial operations across 12 U.S. states, as well as limited international presence in India and Singapore. The company built out a dealer network and pursued sector-specific programs, including discounted pricing for Dairy Farmers of America members on MK-V Dairy models.
Monarch Tractor’s Funding History
A Series of Venture Rounds
Monarch raised capital across multiple rounds, beginning with a $20 million Series A in 2021. The funding trajectory culminated in a $133 million Series C in July 2024, co-led by Astanor Ventures and HH-CTBC Partnership L.P., an affiliate of Foxconn. At the time, the round was described as the largest ever in agricultural robotics and brought total funding to over $220 million, with some estimates reaching approximately $242 million when including grants and smaller additional rounds.
Earlier investors included CNH Industrial and Musashi Seimitsu Industry, alongside At One Ventures and other venture backers.
Key Partnerships
Manufacturing and Distribution
The Foxconn partnership, structured through HH-CTBC, extended beyond investment into manufacturing. MK-V production was relocated from California to Foxconn’s Ohio facilities as part of this arrangement. On the distribution side, Burrows Tractor Inc. became the company’s first official dealer partner in 2023, bringing the MK-V to Pacific Northwest farmers.
Technology and Connectivity
Verizon Business provided connectivity infrastructure to support autonomous operations and data features in the field. A 2025 collaboration with Scout introduced a digital implement offering AI-powered, vine-level mapping and precision viticulture data during tractor operations. Monarch also maintained ties with an India-based AI startup focused on operational insights.
Sector-Specific Programs
The Dairy Farmers of America partnership offered savings and discounts for DFA farmer-owners on MK-V Dairy models, with stated goals around labor efficiency and emissions reduction.
Monarch Tractor’s Deteriorating Position
Layoffs and Workforce Reductions
Cracks began to show in late 2024 when Monarch conducted layoffs affecting more than 10% of its workforce, which PitchBook estimated at around 235 employees at the time. A further wave of up to approximately 100 additional layoffs was reported in late 2025. By early 2026, reports indicated that nearly all remaining staff had been let go.
Legal Challenges and a Reported Pivot
The company also faces multiple lawsuits related to claims made about its autonomous capabilities. Reports indicate Monarch attempted to pivot toward a licensing and software-focused business model, though whether that effort is ongoing or has since stalled is not publicly confirmed.
Headquarters Vacated
By March–April 2026, Monarch had exited its Livermore headquarters — a facility that had served as the company’s primary site for R&D, early assembly, and corporate operations. The property has since been listed for lease and equipment from the site has been auctioned off.
What Remains Uncertain Around Monarch Tractor
The status of Monarch’s intellectual property, technology platform, and any residual corporate activity has not been publicly confirmed. Based on available reporting as of early 2026, the company’s path forward — if one exists — has yet to be disclosed.

Agriculture remains a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, and industry efforts to electrify farm machinery have led to increased consolidation in recent years, including Ideanomics’ acquisition of Solectrac.

Caterpillar Reportedly Acquires Autonomous Tractor Startup Monarch
April 15, 2026

Caterpillar is said to have acquired agricultural technology startup Monarch Tractor, according to a Bloomberg News report citing sources familiar with the matter, signaling a strategic move deeper into automation and electrification.
Monarch recently indicated in a LinkedIn post that its technology had been purchased by a large equipment manufacturer, though it did not identify the buyer. Sources told Bloomberg that Caterpillar was behind the transaction. Neither company has publicly confirmed the deal.
Founded in California, Monarch developed self-driving electric tractors to reduce agricultural emissions. The company has faced operational headwinds in recent months, including workforce reductions, as it struggled to scale its business. As part of its transition, Monarch said it plans to shift away from manufacturing full vehicles and instead focus on licensing its autonomous and electric technology for integration into tractors and other heavy equipment.
The reported acquisition aligns with Caterpillar’s core focus on construction and industrial machinery, where demand for automation and electrified solutions continues to grow.
Monarch’s challenges mirror broader trends in the climate technology sector, where many startups have struggled to convert early innovation into sustainable commercial models. Funding has tightened, and several clean-tech companies have downsized or restructured amid more selective investment conditions.
Venture capital activity in agricultural-focused climate startups has declined sharply from prior highs, according to BloombergNEF, with continued softness into early 2026.
